# Connecting supply of and demand for nutritious foods through a value chain approach: the Thursday Bundle

# 1. Introduction

Urban populations in low- and middleincome countries face growing challenges in accessing healthy diets.

The Nutrition in City Ecosystems (NICE) project works to better connect the local supply of nutritious foods produced using agroecological practices with a growing demand for these foods, even from vulnerable consumers.

## 5. Conclusions

Bringing together supply- and demandside interventions that are accessible to vulnerable consumers is key for transforming food systems – but requires a holistic approach across the entire value chain.

Multisectoral coordination and collaboration, and mutual trust and common understanding between sectors, are central to making such holistic food system initiatives a reality.

# 2. Methodology

In Rangpur and Dinajpur, two secondary cities in north-western Bangladesh, NICE tested the “Thursday Bundle”: curated weekly bundles of vegetables and other nutritious foods, sold in a single package through NICE-supported vendors.

The idea is to make purchasing safe and nutritious food the more convenient and appealing choice when shopping for everyday items. Rather than expecting families to buy various food items for a diverse diet separately and in bulk, the Thursday Bundle brings together selected ingredients in one affordable, hygienically packaged bundle.

Prices of these bundles shall compete with those in local markets, while still providing a livelihood to vendors and producers – thanks to short value chains and coordinated aggregation.

Here we report on the first pilot of 8 weeks between Feb–Apr 2026.

## Food safety and trust were central to the pilot

Vendors explained to customers the benefits of a diverse diet and that the produce were grown without harmful chemicals, using methods such as bio-fertilizers and/or bio-pesticides. The bundles also included QR codes, enabling customers to access further information about the producers and the NICE project in general – building trust through personalization.

## 4. Discussion

• A mix instead of bulk: the bundle lets families buy small amounts of several nutritious foods in one purchase. Buying each item separately often means buying larger quantities – costing more at once and risking that produce spoils before it is eaten.

• Perceived vs. actual price: bundles cost 1–5 BDT less than the same items at market prices, yet “high price” was the most frequent concern. Shoppers are used to spending 10–15 BDT per item across several stalls – one 30–50 BDT payment at a single stall feels expensive, even though it is cheaper.

• Trust drives uptake: explaining nutritional benefits and chemical-free production and QR codes linking to the producers reduced customer hesitation.
